newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French insurer GAN plunges to loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French insurer GAN plunges to loss.

text.p: French state-controlled insurer GAN, hit by fresh property losses, reported on Wednesday a nearly one billion franc ($193 million) first-half loss and warned it would need more state money before being privatised.
GAN, which has already generated a flood of red ink, said its net consolidated loss ballooned to 965 million francs from a loss of 387 million francs a year earlier.
"This result shows the continued deterioration of the real estate market and efforts by the group to clean up its books," the insurer said.

Chairman Jean-Jacques Bonnaud, who forecast last April GAN would break even in 1996, said it would post a full-year loss but "not necessarily double" the first-half figure. "It's clear these losses...are a disappointment," he told a news conference.

The performance reflected losses totalling 1.8 billion francs from GAN's real estate banking activities which Bonnaud warned could hit the same level in the second half. But the insurer showed a recovery in its core insurance operations.
GAN shares closed down nearly one percent at 120.50 francs after being down six percent earlier in the day.

Bonnaud would not say how much more state money the insurer might need to ready it for sale. Last year, he raised the possiblity of the need for a 10 billion franc injection. Since then GAN received a 2.8 billion franc recapitalisation.
GAN is the latest of a series of French state companies to put its hand out to taxpayers ahead of privatisation.
Bonnaud said GAN's sale was still a "realistic possibility (for 1997) if we can do it with the support of our state shareholder". GAN is 80 percent state owned.

But he said GAN needed to put its property troubles behind it before it could be sold. To clean up its property accounts, GAN might sell off some of its distressed real estate to a so-called vulture fund, following the lead taken by other French financial institutions hit by the country's long-running property slump.
Such sales would require further provisions for losses on the disposals that would have to be offset by the state, he said.
He said the state would also have to compensate GAN for any loss suffered on the sale of 67 percent of its banking arm CIC, now in process of privatisation.

The government is considering offers for CIC. But strict conditions on the sale are said to have lessened the appetite for it and there are reports offers by banks BNP and Societe Generale are well below the 14.6 billion franc value in GAN's books.

GAN's banking property arm Union Industrielle de Credit, a longstanding source of problems, made a negative contribution of 799 million francs to group results. Plans for an 800 million recapitalisation of the unit were announced last summer.

But GAN's core insurance business made a profit of 464 million francs after slashing the losses in non-life insurance in France and a big improvement in underlying profits from its French life assurance business. "The insurance results are in line with what was expected. They're even good," said analyst Jerome Labin of French brokerage Pinatton.
GAN's French life assurance operation generated a profit of 425 million francs versus 627 but the figure last time was inflated by one-off gains of 432 million francs.
GAN, France's third largest insurer, made a loss of 1.8 billion francs in 1995. The previous year it recorded a loss of 5.3 billion francs.
